title: Auth Security Essentials: Passwords, Sessions, JWT, MFA and Access Control
summary: Quick revision notes on storing passwords safely (salted bcrypt and argon2), session and JWT authentication, session fixation, MFA, and the broken access control and IDOR bugs that top the OWASP list.

chapters.title: Password Storage Mental Model
points: Hashing is one-way and encryption is reversible: store a slow, salted hash of the password, never the password and never an encrypted copy
A salt is a unique random value per user, stored next to the hash in the clear; it defeats rainbow tables and makes identical passwords hash differently
A pepper is a secret kept outside the database (env var or KMS) and mixed in server-side; it is not stored with the hash, so a DB leak alone is not enough
Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, plain SHA-256) are the wrong tool: a GPU tries billions per second, so use a deliberately slow, tunable password hash
Interview Point: Why is encryption wrong for passwords? What does a salt stop and not stop? Salt vs pepper? Why is SHA-256 alone a bad choice?

chapters.title: bcrypt and argon2 in Practice
points: bcrypt: cost factor n means 2^n rounds, so each +1 doubles the time; tune it to about 250ms per hash (cost 12 is a common start); it generates and embeds the salt itself
bcrypt silently truncates input at 72 bytes, so pre-hash very long passphrases or enforce a maximum length
argon2id is the current default: memory-hard (resists GPU/ASIC attacks), tuned with memory, iterations and parallelism; OWASP minimum is about 19 MiB, t=2, p=1
Usage: hash = await argon2.hash(pw), then ok = await argon2.verify(hash, pw); bcrypt.hash(pw, 12) then bcrypt.compare(pw, hash); never compare hashes with ==
Interview Point: Why is argon2id preferred over bcrypt? What does the bcrypt cost factor do? How do you upgrade hashes when parameters change? Where is the salt stored?

chapters.title: Sessions vs JWT
points: Session: server stores state and the browser holds an opaque random ID in a cookie; revocation is instant (delete the row) but needs a shared store such as Redis to scale
JWT: a signed header.payload.signature token carrying claims (sub, exp); stateless to verify, but the payload is only base64 encoded, not encrypted, so never put secrets in it
A JWT cannot be revoked before exp without a denylist, so use short-lived access tokens (about 15 min) plus a rotating refresh token
Always pin the allowed algorithm and verify the signature: reject alg=none and RS256-to-HS256 confusion, and check exp, iss and aud
Interview Point: When pick sessions over JWT? How do you log out or revoke a JWT? Why is localStorage risky for tokens? What does a JWT signature prove?

chapters.title: Session Fixation and MFA
points: Session fixation: the attacker plants a known session ID in the victim's browser before login; if the server keeps that ID after login, the attacker shares the authenticated session
Fix: regenerate the session ID on login and on any privilege change, invalidate the old one, and never accept IDs from URLs
Harden the cookie: HttpOnly (no JS access), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite=Lax or Strict (CSRF defence), plus idle and absolute timeouts
MFA factors: something you know, have or are; ranking: SMS OTP (weak, SIM-swap) < TOTP app (30s codes, shared secret) < WebAuthn/passkeys (phishing-resistant)
Interview Point: How does session fixation work and what is the one-line fix? What does HttpOnly stop and what does it not? Why is SMS the weakest MFA? How do you handle MFA recovery codes?

chapters.title: Broken Access Control and IDOR
points: Authentication asks who you are; authorization asks what you may do; broken access control (OWASP A01) is a missing or wrong authorization check on the server
IDOR: the app trusts a client-supplied ID, so changing /invoices/101 to /invoices/102 returns another user's data; hidden buttons and UI checks are not security
Fix: on every request check ownership server-side (WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = session.user_id), deny by default, and use the session identity instead of an ID in the request
Random UUIDs only obscure IDs and are not a fix; also check vertical escalation (a user hitting /admin) and horizontal escalation (user A reading user B)
Interview Point: Difference between IDOR and privilege escalation? How do you test for IDOR with two accounts? Why are UUIDs not enough? Where should authorization checks live?

chapters.title: Auth Security Cheat Sheet
points: Passwords: argon2id (or bcrypt cost 12+), unique salt per user, optional pepper, constant-time compare, rehash when parameters change
Sessions vs JWT: opaque ID in a cookie is easy to revoke; JWT is stateless, so use a short exp and a refresh token, pin the algorithm, keep secrets out of the payload
Cookie flags: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax; regenerate the session ID on login and on privilege change to stop fixation
Access control: deny by default, check ownership server-side on every request, use the session identity instead of client IDs, require MFA (prefer WebAuthn) for sensitive actions
Interview Point: Walk through a secure login end to end. What are the top three auth mistakes? How would you audit an API for IDOR?
